summary: Proposes an informal management model for Diffserv routers, defining datapath elements such as classifiers, meters, markers, droppers, queues and schedulers. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3290 gives network managers a shared way to describe how a differentiated-services router handles packets. It divides that work into sorting traffic, checking its rate, marking or dropping packets, and choosing what to send next.

questions: what is the diffserv router management model
subtitle: A conceptual model for configuring and managing Diffserv router traffic handling.

tldr.problem: Diffserv routers can use different internal designs, while network operators need a consistent way to configure and monitor traffic treatment.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3290 models packet handling with classifiers, meters, actions, queues, schedulers and drop algorithms, then groups these elements into Traffic Conditioning Blocks.
tldr.outcome: The model is an abstract aid for management tools. It does not require a particular router implementation or define a formal configuration language.

facts.label: Model elements
facts.value: Classifiers, meters, actions, droppers, queues and schedulers

today: RFC 3290 is an Informational conceptual model for managing Diffserv routers. It is not a formal implementation specification and does not require a particular router design.

sections.title: The Router Model and Its Purpose
sections.content:
Differentiated Services (Diffserv) lets a network offer different service treatment to traffic streams. A packet's Diffserv codepoint (DSCP) indicates a per-hop behavior. Many streams can share a small set of behavior aggregates, which reduces the work required in the network core.

RFC 3290 describes a conceptual model for management and configuration, not a required router design. It represents traffic handling as a connected, directed acyclic graph of functions around a routing core. The model abstracts away vendor-specific implementation details so management tools can describe configuration parameters consistently.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives managers a common description of router functions, even when routers are built differently. It describes how packets move through those functions without requiring routers to use that internal design.

sections.title: Classifiers, Meters and Actions
sections.content:
A classifier sorts one incoming traffic stream into separate streams by matching packet fields or other attributes. A behavior-aggregate classifier uses the DSCP; a multi-field classifier can inspect fields such as addresses, protocol and transport ports. If filters overlap, the configuration must define which one takes precedence.

A meter compares traffic with a rate profile and directs packets to outputs according to whether they conform. Action elements can mark a packet with a DSCP, discard it, count it, or combine streams. Together, these functions describe how the model classifies and conditions traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: A classifier sorts packets by information such as their DSCP or addresses. A meter checks a stream against a rate profile, and an action can mark, count, combine, or discard packets.

sections.title: Queues, Scheduling and Dropping
sections.content:
Queues hold packets until they can be sent and preserve their order in the model. A scheduler chooses which queue supplies the next packet. It may use priority, a minimum or maximum rate, or a bandwidth-sharing rule; a non-work-conserving scheduler can delay packets to shape a stream.

An algorithmic dropper selectively discards packets, often using queue depth or a drop algorithm such as RED. These elements are abstractions: their parameters describe observable behavior and need not map one-to-one to physical queues or hardware in a router.
sections.plainLanguage: A queue holds packets waiting to leave a router. A scheduling function chooses which queue goes next, while a dropping function can discard packets according to a rule.

sections.title: Traffic Conditioning Blocks
sections.content:
A Traffic Conditioning Block (TCB) groups functional elements into a reusable management unit. A TCB can classify, meter, mark, drop, queue and schedule traffic according to a policy. Administrators can connect TCBs in series or parallel and place them at an interface's ingress or egress.

The model has a management hierarchy: individual datapath elements, groups of elements arranged as TCBs, and interfaces that use those TCBs. The RFC gives examples for a customer traffic profile, multiple customers sharing an interface, and per-microflow treatment. TCBs are management abstractions, not physical components.
sections.plainLanguage: A TCB groups router functions into a unit that can express a traffic policy. Managers can reuse and connect these units, then associate them with an interface.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC presents an abstract model and refers readers to the Diffserv architecture for security vulnerabilities in Diffserv operation. It notes that suitable configuration, such as rate-limiting traffic or authenticating traffic marked for higher quality of service, may mitigate some denial-of-service risks.

The document also notes a possible theft-of-service case: a loose token-bucket policer may let a malicious host obtain slightly better quality of service than the traffic profile commits to. The model itself does not prescribe a complete security design.
sections.plainLanguage: Router settings can reduce some risks, such as traffic using more resources than allowed. The RFC also notes that a loose rate check may allow a small amount of extra service.
